t: Find Diameter Endpoints of a Tree — Double BFS
o: A node is special iff it is an endpoint of some diameter path, which in a tree is equivalent to having eccentricity equal to the diameter D. Classic double-BFS: BFS from any node finds a diameter endpoint u; BFS from u finds the other endpoint v and D; then for every node x, ecc(x) = max(dist(u,x), dist(v,x)), so x is special exactly when that max equals D. Example 2: diameter 0↔4 has length 4; nodes 0,4,5,6 all reach distance 4 from u or v.
k: ecc(x) = D ⟺ x is an endpoint of some diametral path.
For diameter endpoints u, v, ecc(x) = max(d(u,x), d(v,x)) — three BFS runs total.

a.i: Run BFS from each node to compute its eccentricity; mark nodes whose eccentricity equals the maximum. O(n²) but conceptually direct.
s: BFS from every source to get eccentricities.
Mark all nodes with ecc = D.

a.i: Two BFS runs find diameter endpoints u, v; a third gives dist from v. The identity ecc(x) = max(d(u,x), d(v,x)) lets us classify all nodes in linear time.
s: BFS from node 0; pick u = farthest node.
BFS from u; pick v = farthest, D = dist(u,v).
BFS from v; mark x special iff max(du[x], dv[x]) == D.

w: State the eccentricity characterization explicitly — it converts a structural question into a distance computation. Pitfall: assuming only the two found endpoints u, v are special (example 2 shows branching creates more); the max-distance formula handles all of them. Follow-up: count diameter paths, or return all nodes lying on any diameter (nodes x with du[x] + dv[x] == D).
